title: Fatal asthma with airway inflammation: long-term inhaled corticosteroid (fluticasone) prevents it
vignette: A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department due to severe shortness of breath. She has no chest pain. The patient does not use tobacco. Temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 132/81 mm Hg, pulse is 102/min, and respirations are 30/min. During physical examination, her condition deteriorates and she is emergently intubated due to acute respiratory failure. Shortly after intubation, she goes into cardiac arrest and dies despite resuscitation efforts. Review of the patient's medical records shows that she had been prescribed multiple medications but had a history of noncompliance. Autopsy shows hyperinflated lungs, airway mucus plugging, and cellular infiltration of the bronchial wall. Long-term use of which of the following drugs would have best prevented the cellular reaction in this patient's airways?

clues.note: Nonadherence to controller therapy is a major risk factor for uncontrolled, potentially fatal asthma.

clues.text: hyperinflated lungs, airway mucus plugging, and cellular infiltration of the bronchial wall
clues.note: Hyperinflation, mucus plugging, and inflammatory CELLULAR INFILTRATION of the bronchial wall are the pathology of uncontrolled asthma - chronic airway inflammation to be prevented by controller therapy.

whatMatters: The 'cellular reaction' is the chronic INFLAMMATORY infiltration of the airway wall in asthma (eosinophils, T cells, mast cells). INHALED CORTICOSTEROIDS (fluticasone) are the most effective long-term controllers - they suppress airway inflammation and remodeling. Answer B.
strategy: Identify the target: prevent the CELLULAR (inflammatory) reaction, not just bronchospasm. Inhaled corticosteroids (fluticasone) are the cornerstone anti-inflammatory controller. Reject bronchodilators/relievers that don't treat inflammation: albuterol (short-acting beta-2 agonist), ipratropium (antimuscarinic), magnesium sulfate (acute bronchodilation), and weaker anti-inflammatory options (montelukast - leukotriene inhibitor, theophylline) that are less effective than inhaled steroids.

eliminations.label: Albuterol - reliever, not anti-inflammatory
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a short-acting beta-2 agonist that relaxes airway smooth muscle. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it relieves acute bronchospasm but does NOT prevent the chronic inflammatory cellular infiltration or airway remodeling. ✅ Correct if: acute rescue of bronchospasm.

eliminations.label: Ipratropium - antimuscarinic bronchodilator
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a muscarinic antagonist reducing vagally mediated bronchoconstriction and mucus. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is a bronchodilator without anti-inflammatory action on airway cellular infiltration. ✅ Correct if: adjunct bronchodilation (COPD/acute severe asthma).

eliminations.label: Magnesium sulfate - acute bronchodilation
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: IV agent for acute severe asthma (smooth-muscle relaxation, mild anti-inflammatory). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is used acutely and is far less effective than inhaled corticosteroids for chronic inflammation. ✅ Correct if: adjunct in acute severe asthma exacerbation.

eliminations.label: Montelukast - weaker anti-inflammatory
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a leukotriene receptor antagonist for long-term control. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it has anti-inflammatory effect but is LESS effective than inhaled corticosteroids at controlling airway inflammation; not first-line to prevent the cellular reaction. ✅ Correct if: add-on/alternative control (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, allergic rhinitis).

eliminations.label: Theophylline - weak, narrow therapeutic index
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a phosphodiesterase inhibitor (bronchodilator with mild anti-inflammatory effect). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is far less potent than glucocorticoids and has a narrow therapeutic index/toxicity. ✅ Correct if: rarely, refractory asthma with careful level monitoring.

reasoning: Autopsy shows chronic inflammatory cellular infiltration of the airway wall (uncontrolled asthma)
Preventing this inflammation requires an anti-inflammatory controller
Inhaled corticosteroids (fluticasone) are the most effective long-term controllers
-> long-term fluticasone would best have prevented the cellular reaction; answer B
mechanism: ASTHMA is characterized by chronic AIRWAY INFLAMMATION (eosinophils, helper T cells, mast cells), airway hyperresponsiveness, and intermittent bronchoconstriction; sustained inflammation causes airway REMODELING (bronchial wall thickening, increased smooth muscle) that worsens obstruction. CORTICOSTEROIDS inhibit production of inflammatory mediators (cytokines, prostaglandins, leukotrienes), reduce leukocyte extravasation into the airway epithelium, induce apoptosis of inflammatory cells, and decrease mucus production - directly preventing the CELLULAR INFILTRATION seen at autopsy. INHALED corticosteroids (e.g., FLUTICASONE) are the cornerstone LONG-TERM CONTROLLER for persistent asthma, reducing exacerbation frequency and severity; nonadherence to controller therapy raises the risk of life-threatening exacerbations. The distractors are bronchodilators/relievers (albuterol, ipratropium, magnesium) that treat bronchospasm without preventing inflammation, or weaker anti-inflammatory agents (montelukast, theophylline) that are less effective than inhaled steroids.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Pulm/Pharm > asthma: chronic eosinophilic airway inflammation + remodeling; inhaled corticosteroids (fluticasone) = first-line long-term controller (anti-inflammatory); SABA (albuterol) = reliever; leukotriene inhibitors/theophylline are less effective controllers.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Prevent airway inflammatory 'cellular reaction' -> inhaled corticosteroid (fluticasone).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on controller vs reliever, inhaled corticosteroid, airway remodeling, eosinophilic inflammation, or leukotriene inhibitor? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Albuterol/ipratropium/magnesium = bronchodilators (no anti-inflammatory control); montelukast/theophylline weaker than inhaled steroids.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: inhaled corticosteroids (fluticasone) are the most effective long-term anti-inflammatory controllers in asthma.

keywords.back: Add-on leukotriene inhibitor (less effective than ICS)

firstAid.detail: Pharm: first-line controller; suppress airway inflammation/remodeling.

memoryHook: Bronchodilators just open the pipe for a moment; only the inhaled steroid (fluticasone) puts out the fire in the airway wall - which is the 'cellular reaction' that kills in uncontrolled asthma.
